text: For a quadratic polynomial ax²+bx+c, its graph can cross the x-axis at two distinct points, touch it at one point (a repeated zero), or not meet it. The x-coordinates of the intersections are exactly the real zeroes of the polynomial.

meta.heading: Polynomials
meta.reviewNote: Cases visually checked against the rendered PDF pages 5–6 and Figs. 2.3–2.5: two distinct crossings give two real zeroes, tangency gives one repeated zero, and no intersection gives no real zero.

text: In a grouped frequency distribution, the class interval with the greatest frequency is the modal class. The exact mode is estimated within that interval using the neighboring class frequencies; it cannot be read directly from the frequency list alone.

text: To find the height of an object above an observer’s eye level, form a right triangle with vertical height h, horizontal distance d, and angle of elevation θ. Then tan θ = h/d, so h = d tan θ. text: For grouped data with equal class sizes, first identify the modal class (the class with the highest frequency). Estimate the mode by Mode = l + [(f₁ − f₀)/(2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)] × h, where l is the modal class lower limit, h is class width, f₁ is modal-class frequency, f₀ is the preceding-class frequency, and f₂ is the succeeding-class frequency.

meta.subject: maths
meta.heading: Statistics
meta.extractiveQuote: “In a grouped frequency distribution, it is not possible to determine the mode by looking at the frequencies. Here, we can only locate a class with the maximum frequency, called the modal class.”
meta.reviewNote: Formula and symbol definitions are printed on rendered original PDF p14; checked denominator and class-frequency order visually.

text: To find the median from a frequency table of distinct observations, arrange the observations in ascending order and form cumulative frequencies. For odd n, the median is the (n+1)/2-th observation; for even n, it is the average of the n/2-th and (n/2+1)-th observations. Use cumulative frequency to locate those positions.

meta.subject: maths
meta.heading: Statistics
meta.extractiveQuote: “Then, if n is odd, the median is the ((n + 1)/2)th observation. And, if n is even, then the median will be the average of the n/2 and (n/2 + 1)th observations.”
meta.reviewNote: Page18 states the odd/even rule; p19 constructs cumulative totals and locates the 50th and 51st values in the example. Both pages rendered and checked.

text: A median of 28.5 marks means that about 50% of the students scored below 28.5 and another 50% scored above 28.5 in the example.

text: For grouped data, a less-than cumulative frequency is the total frequency up to the stated upper class limit: add the current class frequency to the cumulative total for earlier classes. A more-than-or-equal cumulative frequency is found from the overall total by subtracting the frequencies of all classes below the stated lower limit.

meta.subject: maths
meta.heading: Statistics
meta.extractiveQuote: “Similarly, we can compute the cumulative frequencies of the other classes, i.e., the number of students with marks less than 30, less than 40, . . ., less than 100.”
meta.reviewNote: Rendered pp21–22: less-than cumulative frequency sums frequencies through each class; the complementary more-than-or-equal table is formed by subtracting preceding class counts from the total. These are the two forms combined before median-class selection.
